entry: American stealth strategic bomber, operated by the United States Air Force. Designed by Northrop, later [[Northrop Grumman]], with [[Boeing]] as a principal subcontractor, it entered service in 1997 as the second stealth aircraft after the Lockheed F-117 Nighthawk. Development began in 1979 as the Advanced Technology Bomber, a black project. By 1996 the program had produced 21 aircraft at a total cost of $44.7 billion, which made it controversial in Congress. The bomber can carry conventional and thermonuclear weapons and was first used in combat in the [[Kosovo War]] in 1999. The Air Force planned to operate it until 2032.

American aerospace and defense company, headquartered in West Falls Church, [[Virginia]]. Formed in 1994 by the merger of Northrop Corporation and Grumman Aerospace, it is the fifth-largest U.S. federal contractor. In 2024, 87% of its revenues came from the U.S. federal government. Its products include the B-21 Raider bomber, the MQ-4C Triton [[Unmanned aerial vehicle|unmanned aerial vehicle]], and radar for the [[Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II]]. Its defense systems division works on the modernization of the [[Intercontinental ballistic missile|intercontinental ballistic missile]] system, including the LGM-35 Sentinel. The company and its partners have won the Collier Trophy nine times, including for the [[James Webb Space Telescope]].

Ceremonial county of northeast England, bordering [[Scotland]]. It is England's northernmost county and the least densely populated, with 331,420 residents in 2024 across 5,013 sq km. The county's west contains part of the Cheviot Hills, and its highest point is the Cheviot, at 815 m. In the Roman era most of the county lay north of [[Hadrian's Wall]], and centuries of conflict with Scotland led to many castles. During the [[Industrial Revolution]] it had major [[Coal|coal]] mining, [[Shipbuilding|shipbuilding]], and armaments industries.

Sea route north of North America through the [[Arctic Archipelago]], linking the [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]] and [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific]]. European explorers, beginning with [[Christopher Columbus]] in 1492, sought it as a trade route to Asia, but ice blocked them. [[Roald Amundsen]] made the first complete passage entirely by ship in 1903–1906. Until 2009, pack ice prevented regular shipping for most of the year, but sea ice decline, linked to [[Climate change|climate change]], has made it more navigable. Canada treats the waters as internal, while the United States considers them an international strait. In 2016, the Chinese shipping line COSCO sought regular [[Cargo ship|cargo]] voyages through it.

Territory of northern Canada (pop., 2026 est.: 45,904), second-largest and second-most populous of its three territories. Its capital and only city is Yellowknife, the territorial capital since 1967. The territory entered Confederation on July 15, 1870, and its current borders date from 1999, when [[Nunavut]] was created to the east. It has the most interprovincial and inter-territorial land borders in Canada, including [[Yukon]], [[Alberta]], [[British Columbia]], and [[Saskatchewan]]. Its landscape is boreal forest ([[Taiga|taiga]]) and [[Tundra|tundra]].

Nordic country in northern Europe, occupying the western and northernmost parts of the [[Scandinavia|Scandinavian]] Peninsula. Its capital and largest city is [[Oslo]]. The unified kingdom was established in 872, and Norway was part of Denmark–Norway from 1537 to 1814 before a personal union with Sweden until 1905. It was invaded by [[Nazi Germany]] in April 1940 and occupied until the end of the Second World War. Norway is a [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]] and a unitary state, with a population of about 5.6 million. It is a founding member of the [[United Nations]] and [[NATO]], and is part of the Schengen Area. Petroleum accounts for around a quarter of [[Gross domestic product|gross domestic product]], and on a per-capita basis Norway is the world's largest producer of oil and natural gas outside the [[Middle East]]. Its sovereign wealth fund, the world's largest, is valued at US$2.1 trillion.

Marginal sea northwest of [[Norway]], between the North Sea and the [[Greenland Sea]]. Grouped with either the [[Atlantic Ocean]] or the [[Arctic Ocean]], it adjoins the [[Barents Sea]] to the northeast and is separated from the Atlantic by a submarine ridge between [[Iceland]] and the Faroe Islands. Most of its floor is not part of a [[Continental shelf|continental shelf]] and lies about two kilometers (1.2 miles) deep on average. Oil and natural gas deposits are explored commercially in areas up to about one kilometer deep. Its coastal waters are rich in fish, such as [[Cod|cod]]. The warm North Atlantic Current keeps the sea ice-free year-round. Recent research concludes that its large water volume matters more than the Gulf Stream for Norway's mild winters.

Sensory organ and respiratory structure of [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]]. Its external part houses the nostrils, which provide airflow for [[Respiration (physiology)|respiration]]. Behind them, the nasal cavity contains turbinates and olfactory mucosa for the sense of smell and connects to the paranasal sinuses, which buffer pressure and humidify air. Inhaled air is warmed and humidified by capillaries and filtered by hairs and mucus. Odorant molecules dissolve in the mucus, bind to receptors on sensory neurons, and send signals along the olfactory nerve to the brain. In [[Human|humans]] the nose sits centrally on the face, and in [[Infant|infants]] it serves as an alternative airway during suckling. The protruding nose, separate from the [[Mouth|mouth]], is found only in therian [[Mammal|mammals]]. [[Dog|Dogs]] use cold receptors on their wet nose to judge the direction of a smell.

1922 silent horror film directed by [[F. W. Murnau]]. Produced by Prana Film, it is an unauthorized adaptation of [[Bram Stoker]]'s 1897 novel *Dracula*, with [[Count Dracula]] renamed Count Orlok and the story set in Germany. Stoker's widow sued, and a court ordered the prints destroyed, but several survived. Its star, Max Schreck, plays a vampire whose arrival brings plague to a fictional town. The film is regarded as an influential masterpiece of [[Expressionism|German Expressionism]] that helped shape the horror genre. It entered the [[Public domain|public domain]] worldwide in 2019.

French astrologer, apothecary, physician, and reputed seer. Born Michel de Nostredame in [[Provence]], he is best known for *Les Prophéties* (1555), a collection of 942 poetic quatrains allegedly predicting future events. He studied at the University of Avignon and later worked as an apothecary and physician during [[Plague (disease)|plague]] outbreaks. He wrote almanacs, and [[Catherine de' Medici]] became one of his foremost supporters. He suffered from severe [[Gout|gout]] late in life. Many supporters credit him with accurately predicting major events, including the [[Great Fire of London]] and the rise of [[Napoleon]]. Academic sources reject any genuine prophetic ability, arguing that his vague quatrains are later reinterpreted to fit events.

Medieval Catholic cathedral on the Île de la Cité, in Paris, France. Seat of the [[Catholic Church|Roman Catholic]] Archdiocese of Paris and one of the finest examples of [[Gothic architecture]]. Construction began in 1163 under Bishop Maurice de Sully and was largely completed by 1260. Its pioneering rib vaults, flying buttresses, and large rose windows define its design, and it has three [[Pipe organ|pipe organs]] and immense [[Bell|church bells]]. Much of its religious imagery was damaged during the [[French Revolution]]. Interest sparked by [[Victor Hugo]]'s 1831 novel led to restoration between 1844 and 1864. A fire in April 2019 caused serious damage, and the cathedral reopened in December 2024.

City and county town of Nottinghamshire, [[England]]. Historically associated with [[Lace|lace]]-making, bicycles, and tobacco, it received its city charter in 1897 during [[Queen Victoria]]'s Diamond Jubilee. It is the legendary home of [[Robin Hood]]'s enemy, the Sheriff of Nottingham. The city had 323,632 residents in the 2021 census, and its conurbation, the largest urban area in the East Midlands, had 768,638. It is a [[UNESCO]] City of Literature, with links to [[Lord Byron]] and D. H. Lawrence. Nottingham Forest won the European Cup in 1979 and 1980 under [[Brian Clough]].

Capital and largest city of [[Mauritania]], on the Atlantic coast at the edge of the [[Sahara]]. Before 1958 it was a small fishing town. Construction of the planned capital began that year for 15,000 residents, but growth in the 1970s, driven by [[Drought|drought]] and desertification, brought migrants from rural areas. Many settled in overcrowded [[Slum|slum]] districts. By the 1970s the new districts had replaced the old fishing village in importance, hosting government buildings and state enterprises. In 2023 the city had nearly 1.5 million people. It is the hub of the national economy, with a deepwater port and Nouakchott–Oumtounsy International Airport, one of the country's two international airports. Its [[Central business district|central business district]] has broad streets and a grid-like layout.

Part of speech that names a person, place, thing, or idea. In [[Grammar|grammar]], a noun is a lexical category defined by how its members combine with other categories, such as articles and attributive [[Adjective|adjectives]]. Prototypical English nouns are common or proper nouns that can head a noun [[Phrase|phrase]]. Count nouns can be pluralized, while mass nouns are uncountable. In many languages, nouns inflect for number and [[Gender|gender]] or case. The [[Ancient Greek]] term *ónoma* appears in [[Plato]]'s *Cratylus*, and Sanskrit grammarians described word classes from at least the 5th century BC. The English word derives from the Latin *nōmen*, which also covered adjectives. Many modern theories treat [[Pronoun|pronouns]] as a subclass of nouns.

Sudden, temporary brightening of a [[White dwarf|white dwarf]] star in a close [[Binary star|binary]] system. The name comes from the [[Latin]] for "new," describing an apparently new star that fades over weeks or months. Classical novae are the most common type. Hydrogen-rich matter accreted from a companion builds up on the white dwarf until it ignites in runaway fusion, expelling the atmosphere. Recurrent novae repeat every few decades or less. Novae average about ten per year in the [[Milky Way]], mostly near the Galactic Center, but only about one every 12–18 months becomes visible to the naked eye. Unlike a [[Supernova]], a nova leaves its white dwarf intact. [[Tycho Brahe]] described a supernova in his 1572 book *De nova stella*, and the terms were used interchangeably until the 1930s.

Province of [[Canada]] on the east coast. Its name is Latin for "New Scotland," and a 1621 royal charter first used it. Halifax, the capital and largest city, holds over 45% of the population. France founded [[Acadia]] here in 1605, and Britain gained the territory in the 1713 Peace of Utrecht, ending the [[War of the Spanish Succession]]. In 1848 it became the first British colony with responsible government, and in 1867 it joined Confederation. Its economy relies on natural resources, including [[Seafood|seafood]].

Serbian professional tennis player. He holds the record for men's singles [[Grand Slam (tennis)|major]] titles, with 24, and spent a record 428 weeks as world No. 1. He won 102 ATP Tour singles titles and the 2024 Paris Olympic gold medal. In 2016 he became the first man since [[Rod Laver]] in 1969 to hold all four majors at once. He was part of the Big Three with [[Roger Federer]] and [[Rafael Nadal]]. Because of his opposition to the [[COVID-19]] vaccine mandate, he skipped many tournaments in 2022, and he was deported from Australia. He reclaimed the 2023 Australian Open. He led [[Serbia]] to the Davis Cup in 2010. He was named one of [[Time (magazine)|Time]]'s 100 most influential people in 2012.

Independent Russian [[Newspaper|newspaper]], founded in 1993 by former *Komsomolskaya Pravda* journalists and published in [[Moscow]]. It was known for investigative reporting on the Chechen wars and corruption among the ruling elite. Seven of its journalists have been [[Murder|murdered]] since 2000, including Anna Politkovskaya, in connection with their investigations. Its editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov was awarded the 2021 Nobel Peace Prize. [[Mikhail Gorbachev]] used his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize money to help start the paper. After the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, it suspended print, and Russian authorities revoked its media license. It closed on November 9, 2026, citing repression by Russian authorities.

Archipelago (pop., 2024: 2,427) in the [[Arctic Ocean]], off northern [[Russia]]. Its name means "new land" in Russian. It consists of two main islands, Severny and Yuzhny, lying between the [[Barents Sea]] and the Kara Sea. Its northern tip, Cape Flissingsky, is considered the easternmost point of Europe. Russian hunters from Novgorod knew it from the 11th century, and Dutch explorer [[Willem Barentsz]] reached its west coast in 1594. During the [[Cold War]], the [[Soviet Union]] tested nuclear weapons there, including the 1961 air burst of [[Tsar Bomba]], the largest nuclear weapon ever detonated. Its population clusters in Belushya Guba on Yuzhny Island, and the islands are home to [[Polar bear|polar bears]].

Coordinated Islamist terrorist attacks in [[Paris]] and Saint-Denis, France, on November 13, 2015. Three suicide bombers struck outside the Stade de France, and gunmen attacked cafés, restaurants, and the Bataclan. The attacks killed 130 people, and 416 were injured. They were the deadliest in the [[European Union]] since the 2004 Madrid train bombings, and the deadliest terrorist attack in France. The [[Islamic State]] claimed responsibility, saying it was retaliation for French airstrikes in Syria and Iraq. Seven attackers were also killed, and the suspected lead operative, Abdelhamid Abaaoud, died in a police raid on November 18.

Eleventh month of the year in the Julian and [[Gregorian calendar|Gregorian calendars]]. Its name comes from Latin *novem*, meaning nine, because it was the ninth month of the calendar of [[Ancient Rome]]. It has 30 days. It is late autumn in the Northern Hemisphere and late spring in the Southern. The Anglo-Saxons called it Blōtmōnaþ. In Catholic tradition it is the month of prayer for souls in [[Purgatory]]. Its birth flower is the [[Chrysanthemum]] and its birthstone is [[Topaz|topaz]]. [[Meteor shower|Meteor showers]] such as the Leonids peak in November, and in the [[United States]] Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday.

Medieval [[City-state|city-state]] in northwestern Russia, existing from 1136 to 1478. It extended from the Gulf of Finland to the Ural Mountains, with its capital at Novgorod. The republic prospered as the easternmost trading post of the [[Hanseatic League]], exporting furs, wax, and honey. A popular assembly, the veche, elected and dismissed princes, the posadnik (chief executive), and the archbishop. [[Boyar|Boyars]], the landowning nobles, dominated the assembly. The city became subordinate to [[Moscow]] after the 1471 Battle of Shelon, and in 1478 Ivan III dismantled the veche, ending the republic. For much of its history Novgorod was the center of Russian art and culture, notable for its icon painting.

Second-largest city of [[Serbia]] and administrative center of [[Vojvodina]]. Founded in 1694 by Serb merchants across the [[Danube]] from the Petrovaradin Fortress, it was dubbed the Serbian [[Athens]]. Its city proper had 260,438 residents in the 2022 census, and it is the fifth-largest city on the Danube and the largest that is not a national capital. Along with [[Belgrade]], it is an important industrial and financial center. It was a European Capital of Culture in 2022 and became a [[UNESCO]] Creative City of Media Arts in 2023.

Administrative center of Novosibirsk Oblast in [[Siberia]], Russia (pop., 2021: 1,633,595). Founded in 1893 at the Ob River crossing of the future [[Trans-Siberian Railway]], it became Novonikolayevsk in 1895, honoring Saint Nicholas and [[Nicholas II]]. Its rail bridge made it a transport hub, and it developed banks, a power station, and industry. Renamed Novosibirsk in 1926, it grew under [[Joseph Stalin]] into one of Siberia's largest industrial centers. During World War II many factories were relocated there from European Russia. The [[Russian Civil War]] brought typhus and cholera epidemics. It is now the third-most populous Russian city after [[Moscow]] and [[Saint Petersburg]], and is a major [[Science|scientific]] center, home to the Siberian Branch of the Russian Academy of Sciences.

New Year's Day on the [[Iran|Iranian]] calendars, celebrated at the [[Equinox|March equinox]]. Meaning "new day" in Persian, it marks the start of [[Spring (season)|spring]] and usually falls between March 19 and March 22 on the [[Gregorian calendar]]. Its roots lie in [[Zoroastrianism]], and it has been celebrated for over 3,000 years across West and Central Asia, the Caucasus, the Balkans, and South Asia. Most celebrants treat it as a secular holiday, though it remains holy for Zoroastrians, Baháʼís, and Ismaili Shia Muslims. Customs include fire and water rituals, gift exchanges, and poetry recitations. The [[United Nations]] recognized an International Day of Nowruz in 2010. The Iranian calendar was reformed by [[Omar Khayyam]] in the 11th century to fix Nowruz at the vernal equinox.
